screens.title: The Ethereum Ecosystem: Wallets, Nodes, and Networks
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a practical mental model of how wallets, nodes, and networks fit together in Ethereum. A wallet manages cryptographic keys and authorizes transactions; nodes validate and propagate those transactions; networks—Mainnet, Testnets, and local development chains—provide the context where transactions actually run. Understanding these pieces matters because every DApp you build will rely on wallets for identity, on nodes or RPC providers to read and write state, and on networks to control risk during development. For example, when you deploy a contract locally with Hardhat Network you can iterate quickly with instant blocks and no cost. A common misconception is to think a wallet “stores” coins; instead it stores keys that grant control over on‑chain assets. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right wallet type, understand when to run a node versus using an RPC provider, and confidently pick the correct network for development and testing. Consider: what would you lose if your seed phrase were exposed? Keep that question in mind as we explore concrete tools and setups.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

The Ethereum Ecosystem

Learn how wallets manage keys, why nodes are essential infrastructure, and how Mainnet, Testnets and local networks change risk and iteration speed for developers.

Wallets
Manage public/private keys to send and receive ETH. Types include custodial, non-custodial, hot and cold.
Nodes
Run client software to validate blocks. Full, light, and archive nodes serve different roles.
Networks
Mainnet is production. Use Testnets and local chains to test without real value at stake.
Wallet • Node • Network
Wallet (MetaMask)
Stores your keys locally and signs transactions. Used in development to connect to RPC endpoints.
Node (Infura/Alchemy)
Provides RPC access to Mainnet or Testnets without running your own full node.
Network (Sepolia)
A safe test environment that mimics Mainnet behavior using play ETH.
Explore Key Topics
Wallet Types
Custodial vs non-custodial; hot vs cold and their tradeoffs.
Node Roles
Full, light, and archive nodes and why they matter to services.
Networks
When to use Mainnet, Testnets, or a local chain for development.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide practical, secure choices when building on Ethereum. First, you'll be able to distinguish wallet types: custodial wallets store keys for you while non‑custodial wallets return full key control to you. That distinction informs trust and responsibility. Second, you will understand public and private keys: the public key is the address others use to send funds, and the private key is the irreversible secret that authorizes transfers. Grasping this protects you from common security mistakes. Third, you will be able to explain node roles: full nodes verify all state, light nodes minimize storage at the cost of trusting full nodes for data, and archive nodes preserve historical state for advanced queries. Finally, you will learn to differentiate Mainnet from Testnets and local development networks so you never accidentally use real ETH during testing. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can self‑check practical mastery. For example, after this lesson you should be able to explain why you would use Sepolia for testing and when to prefer a cold wallet to hold significant assets.

screens.title: What is an Ethereum Wallet?
screens.narratorSegment: An Ethereum wallet is an interface that manages your cryptographic identity — it does not hold coins, it holds the keys that grant control over funds on the blockchain. The public key, often shown as an address, is what others use to send you ETH. The private key is the secret that proves ownership and signs transactions. Seed phrases are human‑readable encodings of private keys used to recover access. This distinction matters because losing or exposing a private key or seed phrase equates to losing control of the associated assets; there is no central service that can restore access. A concrete example: when you install MetaMask and create a new account, MetaMask generates a seed phrase. You must write it down and store it offline; if you lose your device and wallet without the seed phrase you cannot recover your account. A common misconception is to trust custodial services implicitly because they simplify recovery; remember custodial wallets require trusting a third party. Key takeaway: always know who controls your private key and what that control implies. How will you secure your first seed phrase?

keyIdea.title: Wallet definition
keyIdea.text: Wallets manage keys — public keys receive funds, private keys authorize transactions; seed phrases recover keys.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a Wallet?
Definition

Wallet = Key Manager

A wallet generates, stores, and uses private keys to sign transactions. It may be software or hardware, custodial or non‑custodial.

• Public key/address receives funds. • Private key signs transactions. • Seed phrase restores keys if backed up.
Analogy
Think of a wallet as a set of car keys. The keys open and drive the car, but the car itself exists separately. Lose the keys and you lose access.
Key Takeaway

Do not share private keys or seed phrases. Back them up offline to avoid permanent loss.

Concrete Example
MetaMask Flow
MetaMask generates a seed phrase. You store it offline. MetaMask then signs transactions locally with your private key when you approve them.
Custodial Example
An exchange holds your private keys. This is easier but requires trusting the exchange for security and recovery.
Common Mistake
Treating a wallet like a bank account UI instead of recognizing it as the keeper of keys. That mindset increases risk of accidental exposure.

screens.title: Custodial vs Non‑Custodial Wallets
screens.narratorSegment: Custodial and non‑custodial wallets present a clear tradeoff between convenience and control. Custodial wallets, provided by exchanges or services, hold private keys on your behalf. This simplifies recovery and day‑to‑day use because the service handles backups and password resets, but it introduces a single point of failure: if the service is compromised or imposes restrictions, your funds may be inaccessible. Non‑custodial wallets like hardware devices or browser extensions give you full control of private keys and therefore full responsibility for backing them up and protecting them. For example, using a hardware wallet such as a Ledger keeps your private key offline and safe from browser malware; this is ideal for long‑term storage of significant assets. A common misconception is that non‑custodial automatically means harder to use; modern non‑custodial tools like MetaMask strike a balance with user‑friendly interfaces and clear seed phrase guidance. Key takeaway: choose custodial solutions for convenience when you accept counterparty risk, and non‑custodial when you require sole control and stronger security. Which tradeoff matters more for your project? Custodial vs Non‑Custodial Wallets means custodial = convenience and third‑party trust; non‑custodial = control and responsibility.. In practical terms, tradeoffs: convenience, trust, and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Custodial = convenience and third‑party trust; Non‑custodial = control and responsibility.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Custodial vs Non‑Custodial
Custodial

Service‑held keys

A third party stores and manages private keys. Useful for new users and on‑ramps but requires trust in the provider's security and policies.

• Easier recovery options. • Centralized policies and limits. • Higher counterparty risk.
When to use
Small, frequent trades or onboarding users who value easy recovery over absolute control.
Non‑Custodial

You control the keys

Keys are stored locally or on hardware you control. Gives full autonomy and responsibility for backups and security.

• Full control and no third‑party restores. • Stronger security with hardware wallets. • Must manage backups securely.
When to use
Holding significant assets or when you require sovereignty over keys and privacy.
Key Takeaway

Select custodial when convenience and recovery matter; select non‑custodial for maximum control and security. Balance your project's needs.

screens.title: Public and Private Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Public and private keys are the cryptographic primitives that enable identity and authorization on Ethereum. The private key is a secret numerical value used to sign transactions; the signature proves to the network that the owner authorized the transaction without revealing the private key itself. The public key, derived from the private key, is further compressed into a public address that others use to send funds. For a concrete example, when you create a MetaMask account it generates a private key and shows your public address. If someone obtains your private key or seed phrase they can sign transactions and transfer your funds — there is no password reset. A common misconception is that addresses can be treated as private; addresses are public and visible in block explorers. The security practice is to guard private keys and seed phrases, store them offline when possible, and use hardware wallets for high value holdings. Takeaway: keys are the only proof of ownership on Ethereum — protect them as you would the keys to a bank vault. Public and Private Keys means private keys sign and authorize; public keys/addresses receive funds. never expose the private key or seed phrase.. In practical terms, how keys authenticate and authorize on ethereum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Public & Private Keys
Definition

Private key = signer; Public key = address

A private key is used to cryptographically sign transactions. The public key is derived and displayed as an address to receive funds.

• Signatures prove authorization without revealing secrets. • Addresses appear in block explorers. • Seed phrases allow recovery by regenerating private keys.
Example
Create a MetaMask account to see a public address. The account's private key remains stored locally and is used whenever you confirm a transaction.
Security & Mistakes

Never paste your private key or seed phrase into a website. Treat them as irrevocable secrets. If exposed, funds can be moved immediately by an attacker.

Common Mistake

Typing seed phrases into online forms or storing them in cloud documents can lead to irreversible loss.

Key Takeaway

Protect private keys offline, prefer hardware wallets for large balances, and verify the authenticity of any recovery prompts.

keyIdea.title: Setup steps
keyIdea.text: Install MetaMask, back up the seed phrase offline, enable and switch to Sepolia, and request test ETH from a faucet.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › MetaMask Setup
Steps
  1. Install MetaMask. Add the browser extension for Chrome, Firefox, Brave or Edge and open the welcome flow.
  2. Create a new wallet. Accept terms and write down the seed phrase on paper — store it offline. Never photograph or save digitally.
  3. Enable test networks. In settings toggle show test networks so Sepolia appears in the network list.
  4. Switch to Sepolia. Use the network selector and choose Sepolia Test Network for safe testing.
  5. Get test ETH. Copy the Sepolia address and paste into a faucet to request play ETH for testing.
Example & Check
Example scenario: you deploy a contract to Sepolia and test interactions. Since Sepolia ETH has no monetary value, mistakes won’t cost you real funds. Check your balance after requesting faucet funds and perform a small test transaction to confirm connectivity.
Key Takeaway

Testing on Sepolia is safe and essential. Always back up your seed phrase offline before any testing or deployment.

Common Mistake

Forgetting to check the active network before sending transactions can cause accidental Mainnet operations. Confirm network selection every time.

screens.title: Ethereum Nodes and Their Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Nodes are the infrastructure backbone of Ethereum. A full node stores a complete copy of the blockchain and verifies all blocks and transactions itself. Full nodes participate in network validation and provide the highest security and decentralization. Light nodes store only block headers and request details from full nodes as needed; they are fast to sync and suitable for constrained devices but must trust full nodes for data. Archive nodes store every historical state of the chain, enabling queries about past balances or contract state at arbitrary block heights; they require significantly more storage. For example, a block explorer uses archive nodes to render historical account balances at a given block. Most developers and services use hosted RPC providers that run full nodes so they don't need the resources or maintenance overhead of running their own. A common misconception is that running any node guarantees perfect privacy — while running your own full node improves privacy, other network behaviors can still leak information. Key takeaway: choose node types based on storage, query requirements, and trust model. Ethereum Nodes and Their Roles means full = verify everything; light = minimal storage; archive = historical queries; hosted rpcs offer convenience.. In practical terms, how full, light, and archive nodes differ and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Node selection
keyIdea.text: Full = verify everything; Light = minimal storage; Archive = historical queries; hosted RPCs offer convenience.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Node Roles
Node Types
Full node: stores full chain data, validates blocks and state, highest security.
Light node: stores only headers, queries full nodes for details, fast sync but dependent on full nodes.
Archive node: retains all historical states; required for deep historical queries and explorers.
Example
A block explorer uses archive nodes to answer queries about past contract states, while wallets may use light nodes or RPCs for balance checks.
Considerations
Running a full or archive node requires substantial disk and maintenance. Hosted RPC providers run nodes and expose endpoints so your DApp can read state and submit transactions without this overhead. For privacy and decentralization reasons some teams choose to run their own full nodes despite the cost.
When run a full node
You need to independently verify state, avoid trusting external providers, or serve many clients.
When use RPC
You prioritize speed of development and lower maintenance; accept provider trust and potential rate limits.
Key Takeaway

Match node type to your needs: archive for historical queries, full for independent verification, light for constrained devices.

screens.title: Using an RPC Provider from a DApp
screens.narratorSegment: Your DApp interacts with Ethereum through RPC endpoints. These endpoints speak a JSON‑RPC protocol allowing requests like checking an account balance, reading contract state, or submitting a signed transaction. Hosted providers such as Infura or Alchemy run and maintain full nodes and expose stable endpoints so developers don't need to manage node infrastructure. For a concrete example, a DApp might call the RPC method to get the latest block number or to fetch an account balance. When signing transactions you typically use the wallet to create a signature locally and then send the raw signed transaction via the provider's send endpoint. A common misconception is that using a hosted RPC provider gives you the same privacy as running your own node — it does not; provider operators can observe requests tied to your IP. Key takeaway: use providers for convenience during development, but understand the privacy and trust tradeoffs if your project needs independent verification or high privacy. keyIdea.text: RPC providers expose node functionality over HTTP/WebSocket; they are convenient but introduce trust and privacy tradeoffs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › RPC Usage
How it works

Your app sends JSON‑RPC requests to an endpoint. For reading state the provider responds with data; for writing, the wallet signs transactions locally and the provider broadcasts them.

Illustrative example
POST /rpc
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "eth_getBalance",
  "params": ["0xYourAddress", "latest"],
  "id": 1
}

Response:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": "0xDE0B6B3A7640000"  // balance in wei
}
Notes
• Sign locally: wallets sign transactions so private keys never leave the device. • Providers broadcast: sendRawTransaction is used to submit signed blobs. • Privacy: providers can observe request patterns tied to your app.
Key Takeaway

Use providers for speed and scale, and understand the trust you place in them. Run your own node when privacy or independent verification is required.

screens.title: Block Explorers and Their Uses
screens.narratorSegment: Block explorers are web interfaces that index blockchain data and present transactions, blocks, addresses, and contract code in a searchable way. Tools like Etherscan let you look up a transaction hash to see its confirmations, gas used, and any emitted events. They are indispensable for debugging and auditing because they provide a permanent, public record of on‑chain activity. For example, after deploying a contract to Sepolia you can paste the contract address into Sepolia Etherscan to verify the source code and confirm that your contract was published correctly. A frequent misconception is believing that explorers can alter or hide history; they only reflect the public ledger and cannot change past records. Block explorers also expose internal calls and contract ABI interactions which help developers confirm expected behavior. Key takeaway: use explorers to validate deployments, inspect failed transactions, and audit contract evidence when collaborating or debugging. screens.title: Security Best Practices and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Security rests on two pillars: protecting private keys and verifying environment context before acting. Never share your private key or seed phrase, and never paste them into websites. Back up seed phrases on physical paper stored securely offline. For development accounts, rotate keys frequently and avoid using high‑value accounts for testing. Another common mistake is confusing testnet ETH with Mainnet ETH — testnet funds are valueless and available from faucets, while Mainnet ETH has real monetary value. Also, do not assume hosted RPC providers provide complete privacy; they can observe your activity. When using third‑party services, understand their role: custodial wallets and hosted RPCs trade convenience for trust. A practical example: if a developer uses a single account for testing and production, a leaked seed phrase can compromise both environments. Key takeaway: separate keys by role, back up seed phrases offline, and always verify the active network to avoid accidental Mainnet transactions. Best Practices

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a practical mental model of how wallets, nodes, and networks fit together in Ethereum. A wallet manages cryptographic keys and authorizes transactions; nodes validate and propagate those transactions; networks—Mainnet, Testnets, and local development chains—provide the context where transactions actually run. Understanding these pieces matters because every DApp you build will rely on wallets for identity, on nodes or RPC providers to read and write state, and on networks to control risk during development. For example, when you deploy a contract locally with Hardhat Network you can iterate quickly with instant blocks and no cost. A common misconception is to think a wallet “stores” coins; instead it stores keys that grant control over on‑chain assets. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right wallet type, understand when to run a node versus using an RPC provider, and confidently pick the correct network for development and testing. Consider: what would you lose if your seed phrase were exposed? Keep that question in mind as we explore concrete tools and setups.

These learning objectives guide practical, secure choices when building on Ethereum. First, you'll be able to distinguish wallet types: custodial wallets store keys for you while non‑custodial wallets return full key control to you. That distinction informs trust and responsibility. Second, you will understand public and private keys: the public key is the address others use to send funds, and the private key is the irreversible secret that authorizes transfers. Grasping this protects you from common security mistakes. Third, you will be able to explain node roles: full nodes verify all state, light nodes minimize storage at the cost of trusting full nodes for data, and archive nodes preserve historical state for advanced queries. Finally, you will learn to differentiate Mainnet from Testnets and local development networks so you never accidentally use real ETH during testing. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can self‑check practical mastery. For example, after this lesson you should be able to explain why you would use Sepolia for testing and when to prefer a cold wallet to hold significant assets.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical tasks and safety. You will be able to identify common tools such as RPC providers and block explorers and explain their role: RPC providers give your apps an on‑chain interface without running a node; block explorers let you inspect transactions, addresses, and contract code. Next, you will complete a hands‑on setup: create a MetaMask wallet, back up the seed phrase offline, and switch to a Testnet like Sepolia for safe testing. Third, you will apply security best practices: never share your private key or seed phrase, back it up offline, and verify network selection before signing transactions. Finally, you will learn when to use hosted RPC services like Infura or Alchemy versus running your own node, understanding the tradeoffs in decentralization, cost, and maintenance. Each card includes a mnemonic or mini diagram to help you remember. By practicing these objectives you lower the chance of irreversible loss and increase your ability to develop safely.

An Ethereum wallet is an interface that manages your cryptographic identity — it does not hold coins, it holds the keys that grant control over funds on the blockchain. The public key, often shown as an address, is what others use to send you ETH. The private key is the secret that proves ownership and signs transactions. Seed phrases are human‑readable encodings of private keys used to recover access. This distinction matters because losing or exposing a private key or seed phrase equates to losing control of the associated assets; there is no central service that can restore access. A concrete example: when you install MetaMask and create a new account, MetaMask generates a seed phrase. You must write it down and store it offline; if you lose your device and wallet without the seed phrase you cannot recover your account. A common misconception is to trust custodial services implicitly because they simplify recovery; remember custodial wallets require trusting a third party. Key takeaway: always know who controls your private key and what that control implies. How will you secure your first seed phrase?

Custodial and non‑custodial wallets present a clear tradeoff between convenience and control. Custodial wallets, provided by exchanges or services, hold private keys on your behalf. This simplifies recovery and day‑to‑day use because the service handles backups and password resets, but it introduces a single point of failure: if the service is compromised or imposes restrictions, your funds may be inaccessible. Non‑custodial wallets like hardware devices or browser extensions give you full control of private keys and therefore full responsibility for backing them up and protecting them. For example, using a hardware wallet such as a Ledger keeps your private key offline and safe from browser malware; this is ideal for long‑term storage of significant assets. A common misconception is that non‑custodial automatically means harder to use; modern non‑custodial tools like MetaMask strike a balance with user‑friendly interfaces and clear seed phrase guidance. Key takeaway: choose custodial solutions for convenience when you accept counterparty risk, and non‑custodial when you require sole control and stronger security. Which tradeoff matters more for your project? Custodial vs Non‑Custodial Wallets means custodial = convenience and third‑party trust; non‑custodial = control and responsibility.. In practical terms, tradeoffs: convenience, trust, and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Public and private keys are the cryptographic primitives that enable identity and authorization on Ethereum. The private key is a secret numerical value used to sign transactions; the signature proves to the network that the owner authorized the transaction without revealing the private key itself. The public key, derived from the private key, is further compressed into a public address that others use to send funds. For a concrete example, when you create a MetaMask account it generates a private key and shows your public address. If someone obtains your private key or seed phrase they can sign transactions and transfer your funds — there is no password reset. A common misconception is that addresses can be treated as private; addresses are public and visible in block explorers. The security practice is to guard private keys and seed phrases, store them offline when possible, and use hardware wallets for high value holdings. Takeaway: keys are the only proof of ownership on Ethereum — protect them as you would the keys to a bank vault. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This stepwise walkthrough covers the essential actions to install MetaMask, create a wallet, back up the seed phrase, and switch to the Sepolia Testnet. First, install the MetaMask browser extension for your browser, then follow the create wallet flow which generates a seed phrase. Immediately write that seed phrase on paper and store it offline; do not take a screenshot or store it in cloud storage. Second, enable test networks in MetaMask settings by toggling the option to show test networks. Third, use the network selector to choose Sepolia Test Network. Fourth, obtain test ETH from a Sepolia faucet by copying your Sepolia address from MetaMask and requesting test ETH. Nodes are the infrastructure backbone of Ethereum. A full node stores a complete copy of the blockchain and verifies all blocks and transactions itself. Full nodes participate in network validation and provide the highest security and decentralization. Light nodes store only block headers and request details from full nodes as needed; they are fast to sync and suitable for constrained devices but must trust full nodes for data. Archive nodes store every historical state of the chain, enabling queries about past balances or contract state at arbitrary block heights; they require significantly more storage. For example, a block explorer uses archive nodes to render historical account balances at a given block. Most developers and services use hosted RPC providers that run full nodes so they don't need the resources or maintenance overhead of running their own. A common misconception is that running any node guarantees perfect privacy — while running your own full node improves privacy, other network behaviors can still leak information. Key takeaway: choose node types based on storage, query requirements, and trust model. These endpoints speak a JSON‑RPC protocol allowing requests like checking an account balance, reading contract state, or submitting a signed transaction. Hosted providers such as Infura or Alchemy run and maintain full nodes and expose stable endpoints so developers don't need to manage node infrastructure. For a concrete example, a DApp might call the RPC method to get the latest block number or to fetch an account balance. Ethereum environments come in three flavors: Mainnet, Testnets, and local development networks. Mainnet is the production blockchain where real ETH has value and transactions are irreversible and financially consequential. Testnets like Sepolia mimic Mainnet behavior but use valueless test ETH so you can deploy and test without risking funds. Local development networks, such as Ganache or the Hardhat Network, are personal blockchains running on your machine that provide instant confirmations, deterministic state, and easy debugging. Choose Mainnet only for production-ready code after testing. Use Testnets to validate deployments in an environment similar to Mainnet but safe. Use local networks for rapid iteration during development and unit tests. A common misconception is assuming testnets precisely reflect Mainnet conditions; they approximate behavior but may differ in node count, latency, and gas dynamics. Key takeaway: map your development lifecycle to environments—local for dev, testnet for integration and staging, Mainnet for production—and always double check the active network before executing transactions. Block explorers are web interfaces that index blockchain data and present transactions, blocks, addresses, and contract code in a searchable way. Tools like Etherscan let you look up a transaction hash to see its confirmations, gas used, and any emitted events. They are indispensable for debugging and auditing because they provide a permanent, public record of on‑chain activity. For example, after deploying a contract to Sepolia you can paste the contract address into Sepolia Etherscan to verify the source code and confirm that your contract was published correctly. A frequent misconception is believing that explorers can alter or hide history; they only reflect the public ledger and cannot change past records. Block explorers also expose internal calls and contract ABI interactions which help developers confirm expected behavior. Key takeaway: use explorers to validate deployments, inspect failed transactions, and audit contract evidence when collaborating or debugging. Let's consolidate the most important concepts to remember. First: an Ethereum wallet manages keys — your public address receives funds, while your private key and seed phrase authorize and recover access. Second: wallet types matter — custodial services hold keys for convenience but require trust; non‑custodial wallets put control and backup responsibility on you. Third: node types differ — full, light, and archive nodes trade off storage, verification ability, and historical access. Fourth: choose the right environment — local chains for development speed, Testnets like Sepolia for safe integration testing, and Mainnet only for production. Fifth: RPC providers and block explorers are essential tools — providers expose node APIs for your apps, and explorers let you verify and audit on‑chain activity. Always back up seed phrases offline and double check network selection before signing transactions. These reminders will guide safe and effective development on Ethereum.

Finally, keep three compact rules at hand. One: never share your private key or seed phrase. That single piece of information grants total control over your assets. Two: use environments wisely—develop locally, test on Sepolia, and deploy to Mainnet only after thorough testing and audits. Three: choose infrastructure based on your needs—hosted RPCs for convenience, your own full node for decentralization and privacy, and archive nodes when historical state is required. These rules help you avoid irreversible mistakes, speed up iteration, and select the right tradeoffs for security and operational needs.
